To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
in isolated coronary microvessels changes in pressure and flow, themselves, elicit release and activation of NO and H(2)O(2) via mechanosensitive mechanisms resulting in reactive dilation.

in isolated coronary microvessels changes in hemodynamic factors, i.e., pressure and pressure plus flow, during and following a brief period of occlusion elicit release of nitric oxide and hydrogen peroxide, resulting in reactive hyperemia.
in isolated coronary microvessels reactive dilation elicited by changes in pressure and flow during and after occlusions is mediated by the release of nitric oxide and hydrogen peroxide.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanisms that underlie reactive dilation of isolated arterioles.
the role of hemodynamic forces in eliciting reactive hyperemic dilations.
the role of mechanosensitive mechanisms in the development of coronary reactive hyperemia.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
both hemodynamic and metabolic factors contribute to the eliciting of reactive hyperemia in isolated coronary arteriolar vessels.
the release of NO and hydrogen peroxide (H2O2), which are derived from the endothelium and the smooth muscle cells, are responsible for the reactive dilation of isolated arterioles.
both metabolic and hemodynamic factors contribute to the development of reactive dilations in isolated coronary arteriolar segments.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the release of NO and/or H2O2 during, and after the release of O/R, contributes to the dilation of isolated coronary microvessels.

the mechanisms of reactive dilation in isolated coronary arteriolar vessels involve the release of vasoconstrictors and vasoactive factors during occlusions and release of vasoactivators after release of occlusions.

changes in intralumenal pressure, flow, and shear stress, during and after occlusions, themselves via activation of mechanosensitive mechanisms elicit the release of vasoconstrictor and vasoactive substances that contribute to reactive dilation.
The main takeaway from our work is that

in addition to metabolic factors derived from the cardiac muscle, the changes in pressure, flow, and shear stress, during and after occlusions, themselves via activating mechanosensitive mechanisms elicit release of endothelium-derived vasoactive factors (NO and H2O 2) resulting in reactive dilation.
changes in intralumenal pressure and flow, in addition to metabolic factors, elicit reactive dilation of coronary arterioles.
changes in hemodynamic force, during and after occlusion of coronary circulation, themselves via activating intrinsic mechanisms elicit release of vasodilators resulting in reactive dilation.
